summary: In this episode, Fr. Andrew Stephen Damick and Fr. Stephen De Young conclude their ten-part series on the sacraments of the Orthodox Church by exploring the great blessing of the waters. They begin with a discussion of blood in the Old Testament, tracing its symbolism from Abel's blood crying out from the ground, through the prohibition against eating blood after the flood, to its use in purification rituals and the Day of Atonement. They emphasize that blood represents life, and its shedding in sacrifice brings purification and transformation out of death. They then turn to water, examining its dual nature as both a symbol of primordial chaos and destruction (as in the flood) and a means of purification and life (as in ritual washings and miraculous springs). They connect these themes to Christ's baptism, where He purifies the waters, and to the Orthodox practice of blessing water at Theophany. The episode concludes with a reflection on the Eucharist, where blood and water are combined, and a call to see the sacraments as transformative encounters with God's purifying and renewing grace.

entities.title: Abel
entities.summary: The son of Adam and Eve, murdered by his brother Cain. His blood cries out from the ground for justice, making him a paradigmatic martyr in Jewish and Christian tradition.

entities.title: Moses
entities.summary: The prophet who led Israel out of Egypt, received the Law, and ratified the covenant at Sinai with sacrificial blood. He also struck the rock to bring forth water in the wilderness.

entities.title: Jesus Christ
entities.summary: The Son of God incarnate, whose baptism purifies the waters, whose crucifixion pours out blood and water, and whose blood is the blood of the new covenant. He is the ultimate fulfillment of the sacrificial system.

entities.title: Yam and Nahar
entities.summary: Ancient Near Eastern deities representing the sea and river, symbols of primordial chaos. In the Theophany icon, they are depicted as being subdued by Christ's baptism.

entities.title: Baal
entities.summary: A Canaanite deity associated with storms and fertility, often opposed to Yahweh. The prayer of the Great Blessing of Waters mentions deliverance from the deception of Baal, connecting water purification with the defeat of idolatry.

concepts.title: Blood as Life and Purification
concepts.summary: Blood in the Old Testament is seen as the life of a creature, and its shedding in sacrifice brings purification and transformation out of death. It is used to consecrate objects and people, and its ambivalent nature (life from death) underlies the Torah's sacrificial system.

concepts.title: Water as Chaos and Life
concepts.summary: Water in Scripture has a dual symbolism: it represents primordial chaos and destruction (as in the flood), but also purification and life (as in ritual washings and springs in the desert). This ambivalence is resolved in Christ, who transforms chaos into life.

concepts.title: Great Blessing of Waters
concepts.summary: The Orthodox Christian service of the Great Blessing of Waters, typically performed at Theophany, sanctifies water by invoking Christ's baptism. The blessed water is used for purification and blessing of people, homes, and objects.

concepts.title: Christ Purifies Creation
concepts.summary: Christ's incarnation and baptism purify the material world, which had been subjected to the curse and the power of the evil one. By touching unclean things, He cleanses them, and His blood and water bring redemption and renewal.

claims.text: The blood of the innocent sheds cries out to God for justice, as seen with Abel, and this concept underlies the biblical understanding of martyrdom and divine retribution.
Sacrificial blood is used in the Torah to purify and consecrate objects and people, symbolizing that life (blood) overcomes death (sin's residue).
Water in Scripture symbolizes both primordial chaos and destruction, and purification and life, with Christ transforming chaos into life through His baptism.
Christ's baptism purifies the waters, which had been associated with chaos and death, and this act is emblematic of His incarnation purifying all of creation.
The sacraments are not mere rituals but transformative encounters that purify, renew, and exorcise, requiring active participation and repentance.

scriptural_links.summary: God tells Cain that Abel's blood cries out from the ground, establishing the theme of innocent blood demanding justice.
After the flood, God prohibits eating blood because it is the life of the creature, setting a boundary against predatory behavior.
The ritual for cleansing a house from mildew uses two birds, fresh water, and blood, paralleling the Day of Atonement and providing a biblical basis for house blessings.
God promises to sprinkle clean water on Israel to cleanse them from idolatry, giving a new heart and spirit, connecting water purification with the new covenant.
The piercing of Christ's side brings forth blood and water, which the Church sees as the source of the sacraments of Baptism and the Eucharist.

glossary.definition: The feast of Christ's baptism, celebrated on January 6, when the Orthodox Church performs the Great Blessing of Waters.
A service in the Orthodox Church that sanctifies water, typically performed at Theophany and in the baptismal service, invoking Christ's baptism to purify the waters.
A Lenten service where the Eucharist, consecrated on a previous Sunday, is distributed without a full Divine Liturgy, allowing communion on weekdays during Great Lent.
The annual Jewish ritual (Yom Kippur) for purifying the sanctuary and the people from sin, involving two goats and sacrificial blood.
A German term for the mythological battle against chaos, often depicted in ancient Near Eastern creation stories, but transformed in Genesis where God simply commands the chaos.
